question: Did the trend change when the intervention began, beyond where it was already heading?

lopezbernal2017.cite: Lopez Bernal, Cummins & Gasparrini (2017). Interrupted time series regression for the evaluation of public health interventions: a tutorial. International Journal of Epidemiology 46: 348–355.
lopezbernal2017.checked: every quote and Table 1 read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC5407170) on 20 Nov 2026; the web text has no page numbers, so places are given as the tutorial's steps and sections; in-text reference numbers are left out. Published online in 2016 (the card's year), in the 2017 issue

steps.title: A long series
steps.text: Collect the outcome at regular intervals, for many points before the intervention and many after. Routine data often serve.

quotes.text: A time series is a continuous sequence of observations on a population, taken repeatedly (normally at equal intervals) over time.

steps.title: A clear date
steps.text: The intervention must start at a known time, such as Italy's ban on smoking in public places from 10 January 2005.

quotes.text: ITS requires a clear differentiation of the pre-intervention period and the post-intervention period.

steps.title: Choose the shape first
steps.text: Before looking at the data after the intervention, say what an effect would look like: a drop in level, a change in slope, or both, with or without a lag.

quotes.text: It is important that this decision is made a priori based on existing literature and knowledge of the intervention and the mechanism by which it is expected to act on the outcome.

steps.title: Project the trend
steps.text: Extend the trend from before the intervention into the period after. That line is what would have happened without it.

quotes.text: In an ITS study, a time series of a particular outcome of interest is used to establish an underlying trend, which is ‘interrupted’ by an intervention at a known point in time.

steps.title: Fit the segments
steps.text: Segmented regression fits the trend before, then estimates the jump in level and the change in slope after. In the worked example, admissions for acute coronary events fell by 11%.

quotes.text: β2 is the level change following the intervention and β3 indicates the slope change following the intervention
with a decrease of 11% [relative risk (RR) 0.894; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.864-0.925; P < 0.001)

steps.title: Check the threats
steps.text: Adjust for seasons, and ask what else changed at the same time. Slow-moving confounders sit in the trend; sudden ones do not.

quotes.text: Nevertheless, ITS can be affected by time-varying confounders that change more rapidly. Seasonality can be considered a time-varying confounder

exercise.title: Fit the break
exercise.intro: Monthly hospital admissions for acute coronary events in the tutorial's worked example, 2004–2005, as a rate per 100,000; Italy's smoking ban began in January 2005. Compare a plain before-and-after with segmented regression, then move the break to a month when nothing happened.

quote.text: The hypothetical scenario under which the intervention had not taken place and the trend continues unchanged (that is: the ‘expected’ trend, in the absence of the intervention, given the pre-existing trend) is referred to as the ‘counterfactual’.

exercise.data_label: Real data: the 24 months printed in Table 1 of Lopez Bernal et al. (2017), an excerpt of the 59-month series. Fitted here by ordinary least squares on the rate, without seasonal adjustment, so the numbers differ from the paper's Poisson model on the full series.

limits: The exercise uses only the 24 months printed in the paper's Table 1; the full 59-month series is in the supplementary data, which was not read.
The exercise's straight-line least-squares fit leaves out the paper's Poisson model, population offset, seasonality and autocorrelation checks.

The card's example names heart-attack admissions after a smoking ban; the page uses the tutorial's worked example (data from Barone-Adesi et al.), read only as reproduced in the tutorial. Which region the excerpt covers was not stated in the text read, so none is named.
